endorsements.quote: As there are impactful local factors for many models, the performance of all models should be locally veri fied.

Any non-minor change to workflow, process, definition of an input predictor, or relevant IS software should prompt a veri fication study to demonstrate that there is no substantial impact on model performance.
A quality assurance program should be implemented to detect relevant drifts or shifts in input predictors, outcomes, or the relationship between predictors and outcomes.
Predictor inputs should be compared to the pre-established bounds looking for unexpected outliers , which could include deviations in data type or data values.
All impactful actions should be documented to enable traceability of the entire AICDS process.
There should be a medical director with suf ficient educational background and certification, likely supported by an oversight committee and delegation of some responsibilities.
But, for tools hosted by a third-party vendor, some of the responsibility should fall upon the AI medical director of the provider of the tool.

These requirements could include fully specified procedures, preimplementation verification of clinical performance measures, evaluation of input parameters for local use, assessm ents of algorithmic equity across protected demographic subgroups, and ongoing monitoring for performance drift over time.

In light of the wide variation across hospitals in investment in local AI infrastructure, there is a need for independent, third-party entities to perform accreditation via conscientious and equitable assessments.
The fully deployed process, including automated and manual steps, needs to be fully speci fied in version-controlled policies and procedures.

unlisted_practices: Congress should consider legislation allowing CMS to create CLIA-equivalent certification for clinical practices using AI-based clinical decision support.
CMS should implement AI oversight requirements as a condition of participation and join FDA and ONC in regulating AI application in medicine.
Medicare should reimburse the professional (oversight) and technical (performance) components of AI clinical decision support to drive adoption of safe and effective tools.
Register all AI clinical decision support tools with minimal burden and assign unique tool and version identifiers, labeling outputs with the tool identifier.
Test deployed models regularly, at least on every day of use, against predefined quality control acceptability criteria and release results only if acceptable.
Prevent a model from automatically releasing results when input checks fail pre-established criteria.
Compare model results across peer sites using synthetic patient data, stopping clinical application after serial failures.
Assess competency of personnel responsible for AI model verification, monitoring, and maintenance, and provide them required education and training.
Regularly inspect AI practices by CMS-approved deemed-status organizations, with adaptive inspection requirements.
Avoid applying FDA device-level premarket requirements to locally developed AI tools, preserving local autonomy to develop and refine AI.
Evaluate all AI models for effectiveness, retrospectively and ideally prospectively and pragmatically, relative to key clinical outcomes.
Define bounds for model outputs and requirements for evaluating appropriateness of inputs for AI tools with broad indications.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/commentary proposing an AI oversight framework for healthcare organizations modeled after clinical laboratory regulations.
